title: WHAT THE CONTAINER SCHEME COSTS CRAFT DISTILLERS
summary: Bevan asked whether the Government has assessed or modelled what the Container Deposit Scheme costs Western Australian craft distillers, on top of Commonwealth excise, and whether any relief was considered. The Government said it treated the expansion as a scheme-wide reform, had not engaged the Commonwealth, and holds no assessment of the impact on craft distillers to table.
ask: Whether the Government has assessed the interaction between Container Deposit Scheme obligations and Commonwealth excise for spirits producers, modelled the per-container cost at different production volumes, engaged the Commonwealth, Treasury or the ATO, considered any exemption, rebate or transitional arrangement, and met with the WA Distillers Guild, and whether it will table that work.
answer: The Government said the expansion was considered as a scheme-wide reform and that a consultation summary has been published on the Western Australian Government website. It said the supplier contribution rate is defined by container material type rather than production volume, and that these rates are published by the Scheme Coordinator. Asked whether it had engaged the Commonwealth Government, Treasury or the Australian Taxation Office on the interaction between excise obligations and the scheme, it answered no. Asked whether it would table any briefing, advice or assessment relating to the impact of the scheme on Western Australian craft distillers, it answered no. It said measures developed to support new first responsible suppliers included annual reporting obligations for suppliers of fewer than 150,000 units, streamlined container approval processes, and extended transitional periods for labelling requirements. It said representatives of WA Distillers Guild Inc participated in a meeting of the Department's Stakeholder Advisory Group on 16 October 2025, and were invited to meetings on 24 November 2025 and 5 March 2026 but did not attend.
finding: The Government confirmed it never contacted the Commonwealth about how the scheme interacts with spirits excise, and holds no assessment of the impact on Western Australian craft distillers to table. The support measures it listed are administrative, and none reduces the cost a distiller pays.

title: HAS WA DISTILLING'S VALUE BEEN MEASURED
summary: Bevan asked whether the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development had measured the economic contribution of the craft distilling sector and the impact of the Container Deposit Scheme on it. The Government sent the first part to another Minister and answered the rest by referral.
ask: Whether DPIRD has assessed the economic contribution of the WA craft distilling sector, including regional employment, tourism expenditure, exports and use of WA agricultural inputs, whether it has assessed the impact of Container Deposit Scheme obligations on distilleries' profitability, investment, employment and tourism, whether any grant, rebate or transition assistance was considered, and whether it has met with the WA Distillers Guild, with the underlying briefings and modelling tabled.
answer: The Government said questions relating to engagement between the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development and the Western Australian craft distilling sector should be directed to the Minister for Agriculture and Food. It answered the remaining parts by referring to its answer to Legislative Assembly Question on Notice 2576.
finding: The question of the distilling sector's economic contribution was passed to another Minister, and the questions on impact, assistance and tabling were answered by referral. No assessment was produced.

title: WAS DISTILLING ASSESSED BEFORE SPIRITS WENT IN
summary: Bevan asked whether an industry-specific impact assessment was undertaken for the distilling sector before spirits containers were included in the scheme, and if not, why not. The Government answered by referring to another question.
ask: Whether an industry-specific impact assessment was undertaken for the Western Australian distilling sector before the decision to include spirits containers in the Container Deposit Scheme from 1 July 2026, on what date any such assessment was completed and whether it will be tabled, and if no assessment was undertaken, why not.
answer: The Government answered both parts by referring to its answer to Legislative Assembly Question on Notice 2576.
finding: A direct question on whether an industry-specific assessment was done, and why not, was answered by referral. The referred answer states the expansion was treated as a scheme-wide reform.

title: HAS THE WINE PRODUCERS' CDS CONTRACT BEEN CHECKED
summary: Bevan asked when the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation reviewed the standard-form Supply Agreement issued to wine producers, who conducted the review and whether the briefing would be tabled. The Government said the CEO approved the agreement on 13 May 2026 and that no briefing material can be provided.
ask: Whether the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation has reviewed the standard-form Supply Agreement that WA Return Recycle Renew Ltd (WARRRL) issues to wine producers for the Container Deposit Scheme, when and by whom, whether that review examined the unilateral-variation, modern-slavery, audit, statutory-declaration and confidentiality provisions and identified any needing amendment or further consultation, and whether the Minister will table any departmental briefing or advice on the agreement.
answer: The Government said the Supply Agreement is subject to government oversight and must be approved by the CEO of the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation under the Waste Avoidance and Resource Recovery (Container Deposit Scheme) Regulations 2019. It said the agreement was approved by the CEO on 13 May 2026, and that the review was conducted by the Department's Circular Economy and Legal Services Directorates. It said the review and approval considered all provisions in the Supply Agreement, and that the Department considers the agreement appropriately reflects the rights and obligations of the parties and provides the necessary consistency and certainty for all suppliers. It said that because the CEO has statutory responsibility for approving the agreement, no briefing material can be provided concerning it.
finding: The Supply Agreement was approved on 13 May 2026, 49 days before producers were bound by it on 1 July 2026. The Government says every provision was considered, and that no briefing on it can be provided.

title: HAVE WINE PRODUCERS HAD TIME TO SIGN UP
summary: Bevan asked how many wine producers had signed a Supply Agreement, how many were expected to, and whether a plain-English summary of their obligations had been published. The Government said it does not hold data allowing a reliable count, and pointed to a template published since 2020.
ask: How many wine producers have executed a supply agreement with WARRRL and how many are WA-based versus interstate, how many are expected to need one before 1 July 2026 and what proportion have signed, whether WARRRL assessed if producers have sufficient time to receive the agreement, obtain independent legal advice and execute it before the deadline, and whether a plain-English summary of producer obligations has been published.
answer: The Government said the Container Deposit Scheme does not maintain suppliers in categories based solely on beverage type, that many first responsible suppliers supply multiple beverage categories, and that the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation does not hold data that would enable a reliable count of suppliers that are exclusively or primarily wine producers. It said all first responsible suppliers are expected to have a valid Supply Agreement. It said the Department is aware suppliers have had access to the agreement prior to commencement of the expanded arrangements and have been able to obtain independent legal advice if they choose to do so, that it considers suppliers have been provided with information, and that the Supply Agreement template has been published on the WA Return Recycle Renew Ltd website since scheme commencement in 2020.
finding: The Government cannot say how many wine producers were required to sign, or how many had signed before the scheme began. Its answer on time for legal advice rests on a template published in 2020, while the agreement producers had to sign was approved on 13 May 2026. Whether a plain-English summary of obligations exists was not answered.

title: CAN PRODUCERS SHOW THE CDS CONTRACT TO ADVISERS
summary: Bevan asked whether the confidentiality clause in the Supply Agreement lets producers show it to their lawyer, accountant or industry association, and whether the Government had reviewed the clause. The Government declined to answer, citing Standing Order 77(2).
ask: Whether clause 14.1 of the WARRRL supply agreement restricts disclosure of its contents without WARRRL's written consent, whether it permits disclosure to legal advisers, accountants, financial advisers and industry associations and on what conditions, whether the Government has reviewed the clause's impact on access to professional advice and collective industry consultation, and whether the Minister will table any advice on the confidentiality provisions.
answer: The Government said the questions seek a legal interpretation of the terms and operation of the Supply Agreement, and that Standing Order 77(2) provides that questions should not seek legal interpretation or opinion.
finding: No part was answered. Two of the four parts asked whether the Government had reviewed the clause and whether it would table any advice on it, which ask whether something happened rather than what a clause means.

title: CAN PRODUCERS SPEAK PUBLICLY ABOUT THE SCHEME
summary: Bevan asked whether the communication protocols producers must comply with have been finalised and provided to them, and whether they restrict what producers may say publicly about scheme costs. The Government said the clause reference did not identify a document.
ask: Whether clause 14.3 of the WARRRL supply agreement requires producers to comply with communication protocols issued by WARRRL, whether those protocols have been finalised and provided to all producers expected to execute an agreement, whether they regulate or restrict public statements by producers about scheme costs, administration and compliance obligations, and whether the Minister will table the current protocols.
answer: The Government said the reference to clause 14.3 does not identify what document it refers to and that it is therefore not possible to answer the question.
finding: Whether the protocols exist, when they were finalised and whether producers have received them was not answered. The Government answered questions about other clauses of the same agreement on the same day.

title: HOW FAR CAN WARRRL AUDIT WINE PRODUCERS
summary: Bevan asked what notice producers get before an audit, what limits apply to audits and what they cost to comply with. The Government said the clause reference did not identify a document, and confirmed no separate assessment of the audit provisions was undertaken.
ask: Whether clause 7.5 of the WARRRL supply agreement permits WARRRL to audit producers' scheme records, whether the agreement prescribes a minimum notice period before an audit and any limit on the frequency, duration and categories of records that may be examined, whether the Government has assessed the compliance cost of those audit requirements, and whether the Minister will table any policy or protocol governing WARRRL's audit powers.
answer: The Government said the reference to clause 7.5 does not identify what document it refers to and that it is therefore not possible to answer that question. On the remaining parts it said audit and assurance requirements form part of the overall governance and integrity framework supporting the operation of the scheme, that a separate assessment has not been undertaken in relation to audit provisions specifically, and that audit activity must relate to the supplier's obligations under the Supply Agreement and the operation of the scheme.
finding: The Government confirmed it has never assessed what the audit requirements cost producers. The notice period, the limits on frequency and duration, and the categories of records that may be examined were not stated.

title: PERSONAL LEGAL RISK ON WINERY DIRECTORS
summary: Bevan asked about the annual statutory declaration a company director must sign, the burden it places on small and micro wine producers and the legal risk to directors. The Government used Standing Order 77(2), a referral and legal professional privilege across three parts of the one question.
ask: Whether clause 7.1(b) of the WARRRL supply agreement requires a director of a corporate producer to provide an annual statutory declaration verifying the accuracy of information given to WARRRL, whether the Government has assessed the compliance burden of that requirement for small and micro wine producers and what it concluded, whether it has received advice on the legal risks to directors arising from it, and whether the Minister will table any assessment or advice on the statutory-declaration requirement.
answer: The Government said the first two parts seek a legal interpretation of the terms and operation of the Supply Agreement and that Standing Order 77(2) provides questions should not seek legal interpretation or opinion. It answered the question on compliance burden by referring to its answer to Legislative Assembly Question on Notice 2576. It said whether or not independent legal advice has been sought in relation to any matter is subject to legal professional privilege.
finding: Three different grounds were used to avoid three parts of one question. The burden on small and micro producers of a director signing an annual statutory declaration remains unassessed.

title: MODERN SLAVERY RULES MEANT FOR $100M FIRMS
summary: Bevan asked what the modern slavery obligations in the Supply Agreement cost producers, and whether they exceed what Commonwealth law requires of most Western Australian wine producers. The Government declined most parts under Standing Order 77(2) and said wine inclusion was a 2025 election commitment.
ask: Whether clause 8 of the WARRRL supply agreement requires wine producers to implement modern-slavery compliance measures, warrant against modern-slavery risks in their supply chains and impose equivalent obligations on their own suppliers, whether the Government has assessed the annual compliance cost of those obligations per producer, whether it accepts the Commonwealth Modern Slavery Act 2018 generally applies only to entities with revenue of at least $100 million, whether it has assessed if clause 8 exceeds what would otherwise apply to most WA wine producers, and whether the Minister will table any assessment or advice on the modern-slavery obligations.
answer: The Government said parts 1 to 3 and parts 5 to 7 seek a legal interpretation of the terms and operation of the Supply Agreement, and that Standing Order 77(2) provides that questions should not seek legal interpretation or opinion. On compliance costs it said the State Government considered the expansion of the Container Deposit Scheme as a whole and undertook consultation and engagement across affected industry sectors as a policy development process, that the obligation to participate applies to all first responsible producers who supply into the Western Australian market regardless of where they produce, and that the inclusion of wine bottles was an election commitment made by the Cook Labor Government at the 2025 State Election which the expansion on 1 July 2026 gave effect to.
finding: The part asking the revenue threshold in the Commonwealth Modern Slavery Act 2018 was refused as seeking interpretation of the Supply Agreement. No estimate of the compliance cost to a producer was given, and the Government's stated basis for the obligation is the election commitment.

title: CAN THE SCHEME PRICE RISE WITHOUT A CAP
summary: Bevan asked whether the Supply Agreement caps the Scheme Price producers pay, whether it can be amended on ten business days' notice, and who carries the financial risk of future changes. The Government declined to answer, citing Standing Order 77(2).
ask: Whether the supply agreement permits WARRRL to determine the scheme price and whether it specifies any maximum price, fixed formula or cap on future increases, whether clause 10.2(c) permits amending the payments schedule on 10 business days' notice and clause 9 permits amending the agreement after legislative or coordinator-agreement changes with no compensation to producers for resulting losses, whether the Government considers producers bear the financial risk of future regulatory changes, and whether the Minister will table any assessment of those financial risks.
answer: The Government said the questions seek a legal interpretation of the terms and operation of the Supply Agreement, and that Standing Order 77(2) provides that questions should not seek legal interpretation or opinion.
finding: No part was answered, including the request to table any assessment of the financial risk the agreement places on producers, which asks whether a document exists rather than what a clause means.

title: WHAT PRODUCER DATA CAN WARRRL DISCLOSE
summary: Bevan asked what producer information WA Return Recycle Renew Ltd may disclose, including payment, sales and container volumes, and whether producers are told before they sign. The Government said the clause reference did not identify a document.
ask: Whether clause 7.8 of the WARRRL supply agreement authorises WARRRL to disclose information obtained from producers, what categories of information may be disclosed, whether that includes producer payment information, sales volumes, container volumes and compliance information, whether producers are given written advice before signing identifying what may be disclosed, and whether the Minister will table any policy or protocol governing disclosure of producer information under clause 7.8.
answer: The Government said the reference to clause 7.8 does not identify what document it refers to and that it is therefore not possible to answer the question.
finding: Producers were not told what commercial information about them may be disclosed, and whether they are advised of it before signing was not answered.

title: WILL WA PAUSE BEFORE WINE GOES FIRST
summary: Bevan asked whether the Government had assessed the competitive impact on Western Australian wine producers, whether it would ask for the Supply Agreement to be reviewed, and whether it would support a 12 month deferral. The Government answered all five parts by referring to another question.
ask: Whether the Government has assessed the competitive impact on WA wine producers of including wine bottles in the Container Deposit Scheme from 1 July 2026, whether it has assessed the extent to which producers in Victoria, New South Wales, South Australia and Tasmania will face equivalent obligations before 1 July 2027, whether it has assessed the cumulative compliance burden of the supply-agreement, modern-slavery, audit, statutory-declaration and reporting obligations, whether it will request WARRRL to review the agreement before 1 July 2026, and whether it will support a 12-month deferral of wine's inclusion or, if not, what specific measures it will implement before 1 July 2026 to address producers' concerns.
answer: The Government answered all parts by referring to its answer to Legislative Assembly Question on Notice 2604.
finding: The referred answer does not address competitive impact, interstate timing, the cumulative compliance burden or a deferral. None of the five parts was answered.

title: HAS THE MINISTER EVEN SEEN THE AGREEMENT
summary: Bevan asked when the Minister first received the Supply Agreement, when the Department reviewed it and whether the briefing would be tabled. The Government answered by referring to another question.
ask: Whether the Minister has received a copy of the WARRRL supply agreement to be executed by wine producers before 1 July 2026 and on what date, whether the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation has reviewed the agreement and when, whether that review specifically considered clause 8 (modern slavery), clause 9 (variation), clause 7.5 (audits), clause 7.1(b) (statutory declarations) and clause 14 (confidentiality and communications), and whether the Minister will table any briefing, review or advice concerning the agreement.
answer: The Government answered all parts by referring to its answer to Legislative Assembly Question on Notice 2579.
finding: The referred answer gives the date the CEO approved the agreement but does not say when the Minister first received it. That date remains unstated.

title: HOW MANY HAVE SIGNED, AND ON WHAT TIMETABLE
summary: Bevan asked how many wine producers had signed a Supply Agreement, what share that represented, and whether WA Return Recycle Renew Ltd had given the Government a timetable for the rest. The Government said it holds no reliable count and has no timetable.
ask: How many wine producers have executed a supply agreement with WARRRL, how many are expected to need one before 1 July 2026 and what percentage have signed, whether WARRRL has provided the Government with a forecast execution timetable for the remaining producers and whether it will be tabled, and whether the Government has assessed whether producers have sufficient time to obtain independent legal advice before 1 July 2026.
answer: The Government said the Container Deposit Scheme does not maintain suppliers in categories based solely on beverage type and that many first responsible suppliers supply multiple beverage categories. It said all first responsible suppliers are expected to have a valid Supply Agreement, and that the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation does not hold data that would enable a reliable count of suppliers that are exclusively or primarily wine producers and is unable to provide the percentage requested. Asked whether WA Return Recycle Renew Ltd had provided the Government with a forecast execution timetable for remaining producers, it answered no. It answered the question on time for legal advice by referring to Legislative Assembly Question on Notice 2584.
finding: The Government could not say how many producers had signed or what share that represented, and had not obtained a timetable from the scheme coordinator for the remainder.

title: DO CLAUSE 8'S DUTIES EXCEED FEDERAL LAW
summary: Bevan asked what the modern slavery obligations cost producers and whether they exceed what Commonwealth law requires. The Government said the clause reference did not identify a document.
ask: Whether clause 8 of the WARRRL supply agreement requires wine producers to implement modern-slavery compliance measures, warrant against modern-slavery risks in their supply chains and impose equivalent obligations on suppliers and contractors, whether the Government has assessed the estimated annual compliance cost per producer, whether it has assessed if clause 8 imposes obligations exceeding those that would otherwise apply to most WA wine producers under Commonwealth legislation and with what outcome, and whether the Minister will table any assessment relating to clause 8.
answer: The Government said the reference to clause 8 does not identify what document it refers to and that it is therefore not possible to answer the question.
finding: On the same day the Government answered a question about clause 8 of the Supply Agreement by citing Standing Order 77(2), a ground that depends on knowing which document the clause sits in. Here it said the document could not be identified.

title: NO CAP, NO COMPENSATION, ALL THE RISK
summary: Bevan asked whether the Supply Agreement sets any maximum Scheme Price or cap on increases, and whether producers can be left without compensation when it is amended. The Government declined most parts under Standing Order 77(2) and referred the rest.
ask: Whether the supply agreement specifies no maximum scheme price and no cap on future price increases, whether clause 10.2(c) permits amending the payments schedule on 10 business days' notice, whether clause 9 permits amending the agreement after legislative or coordinator-agreement changes with no entitlement to compensation for resulting losses, and whether the Government has assessed the financial risk to producers arising from clauses 9 and 10 and will table that assessment.
answer: The Government said parts 1 to 5 seek a legal interpretation of the terms and operation of the Supply Agreement and that Standing Order 77(2) provides questions should not seek legal interpretation or opinion. It answered the question on financial risk by referring to its answer to Legislative Assembly Question on Notice 2576.
finding: Whether there is any ceiling on what producers can be charged was not answered, and the referred answer contains no assessment of the financial risk they carry.

title: WHAT LIABILITY DOES A SIGNING DIRECTOR CARRY
summary: Bevan again asked whether the Government has assessed the legal risk and director liability created by the annual statutory declaration in clause 7.1(b), and whether it has any advice on it to table. Awaiting the Government's reply.
ask: Whether clause 7.1(b) of the WARRRL supply agreement requires a director of a corporate producer to execute an annual statutory declaration relating to information previously supplied to WARRRL, whether the Government has assessed the legal risks associated with that requirement, whether it has received any advice on potential liability for directors arising from clause 7.1(b), and whether the Minister will table any such assessment or advice.
answer: Not yet answered. This question was asked on 9 June 2026 and the Government's reply is still outstanding.
finding: The question again tests what personal legal liability a winery director takes on by signing, and whether the Government has any advice on it, and awaits the Government's response.

title: WHAT CAN PRODUCERS SAY, AND TO WHOM
summary: Bevan asked whether the confidentiality clause restricts disclosure of the Supply Agreement, and whether the communication protocols have been finalised and given to producers. The Government cited Standing Order 77(2), then directed the member to WA Return Recycle Renew Ltd as a private company.
ask: Whether clause 14.1 of the WARRRL supply agreement restricts disclosure of the agreement without WARRRL's written consent, whether clause 14.3 requires producers to comply with communication protocols issued by WARRRL, whether those protocols have been finalised and provided to all producers expected to execute the agreement, and whether the Minister will table the communication protocols.
answer: The Government said the first two parts seek a legal interpretation of the terms and operation of the Supply Agreement and that Standing Order 77(2) provides questions should not seek legal interpretation or opinion. On the communication protocols it said these questions relate to documents owned and controlled by WA Return Recycle Renew Ltd, and that access should be sought from WARRRL, who are a privately run company.
finding: Documents that govern what producers may say publicly about a statutory scheme were placed beyond Parliament's reach on the basis that the scheme coordinator is a private company.

title: WILL THE GOVERNMENT DEFER WINE FOR A YEAR
summary: Bevan asked whether the Government had assessed the economic impact of including wine bottles in the scheme and the cumulative compliance burden on producers, and whether it would support a 12 month deferral. The Government said it did not undertake separate sector-by-sector impact assessments.
ask: Whether the Government has assessed the economic impact of including wine bottles in the Container Deposit Scheme from 1 July 2026, whether it has assessed the cumulative compliance burden of the supply-agreement, reporting, statutory-declaration and modern-slavery obligations and will table those assessments, whether it will request WARRRL to review the agreement before 1 July 2026, and whether it will support a 12-month deferral of wine's inclusion or, if not, what specific actions it will take before 1 July 2026 to address producers' concerns.
answer: The Government said the State Government did not undertake separate sector-by-sector impact assessments but rather considered the expansion as a scheme-wide reform, which included public consultation, targeted industry engagement, workshops and advice from a Stakeholder Advisory Group comprising representatives from the beverage, retail, waste and recycling sectors, and that a consultation summary has been published on the Western Australian Government website. It said the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation considers the current Supply Agreement appropriately reflects the rights and obligations of the parties and provides the necessary consistency and certainty for all suppliers. It answered the question on a 12 month deferral by referring to its answer to Legislative Assembly Question on Notice 2604.
finding: The Government confirmed it never assessed the impact on the wine sector, treating the expansion as a scheme-wide reform. The advisory group it relied on is described as representing the beverage, retail, waste and recycling sectors. The deferral question was referred to an answer that does not address it.

title: HAS THE HIT TO WINE REGIONS BEEN ASSESSED
summary: Bevan asked whether the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development had assessed the impact of wine inclusion on regional employment, tourism, exports and economic activity, or modelled the cost to producers in nine named wine regions. The Government answered no.
ask: Whether DPIRD has assessed the impact of including wine in the Container Deposit Scheme on regional employment, regional tourism, wine exports and regional economic activity, whether it has modelled the impact of scheme costs on wine producers across the Margaret River, Great Southern, Geographe, Blackwood Valley, Southern Forests, Swan Valley, Perth Hills, Peel and Pemberton-Manjimup regions and will table any such assessment or modelling, and if none was undertaken, what information it relied on to determine the regional impacts of wine inclusion were acceptable.
answer: The Government answered both parts no.
finding: No assessment and no modelling was done of what the Container Deposit Scheme would do to regional employment, regional tourism, wine exports or regional economic activity, in Margaret River, Great Southern, Geographe, Blackwood Valley, Southern Forests, Swan Valley, Perth Hills, Peel or Pemberton-Manjimup.

title: DID THE MINISTER PUSH FOR WINE RELIEF
summary: Bevan asked whether the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development had advised any Minister on how the Wine Equalisation Tax affects the cost of the scheme, and whether the Minister pushed for a deferral or relief. The Government answered no on the advice and did not say what the Minister sought.
ask: Whether DPIRD provided advice to Cabinet or any Minister on the impact of the Wine Equalisation Tax on the effective cost of the Container Deposit Scheme for wine producers and will table it, whether DPIRD assessed the competitive impact on WA wine producers of wine inclusion occurring ahead of equivalent reforms in South Australia, Victoria and New South Wales, and whether the Minister advocated within Government for a deferral of wine inclusion, transitional assistance and a small-producer relief mechanism, what action was taken, and if not, why not.
answer: Asked whether the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development provided advice to Cabinet, the Minister for Environment or any other Minister regarding the impact of the Wine Equalisation Tax on the effective cost of the scheme for wine producers, the Government answered no. On the remaining parts it said the Minister for Regional Development has been involved in a range of discussions about the expansion of the Container Deposit Scheme, and that a range of other jurisdictions including South Australia, New South Wales, Queensland, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory have expanded or committed to expanding their schemes to include wine and spirit bottles.
finding: No advice was given to any Minister on how the Wine Equalisation Tax compounds the cost of the scheme for wine producers. The Government did not say whether the Minister sought a deferral, transitional assistance or a small producer relief mechanism, and its list of other jurisdictions carries no commencement dates and does not include Victoria or Tasmania.

title: WHO WAS CONSULTED, AND WHAT SUPPORT OFFERED
summary: Bevan asked for the dates and attendees of meetings with wine industry representatives since January 2024, and what support measures had been considered. The Government directed the matter to another Minister and said no material on support measures has been produced.
ask: What formal meetings on Container Deposit Scheme expansion have occurred since 1 January 2024 between the Minister for Environment, DPIRD, Regional Development Commissions and representatives of Wines of Western Australia, regional wine associations and individual producers, and the date, attendees and purpose of each, whether the Government has considered any rebate, grant, transitional assistance or small-producer support for wine producers and what options, whether DPIRD has prepared any briefing or options paper on support measures for the wine industry and will table it, and whether the Minister intends to establish any industry reference or working group to monitor the scheme's impact on regional wine communities.
answer: The Government said the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development meets regularly with stakeholders pertaining to departmental matters, that matters regarding the Western Australian container deposit scheme should be directed to the Minister for the Environment, and that no material has been produced by the Department regarding support measures.
finding: No meeting dates or attendees were provided, and the department responsible for the regional economy confirmed it has produced no material at all on support measures for the wine industry.

title: WHO KEEPS WARRRL ACCOUNTABLE
summary: Bevan asked what the Government had done with the findings of the Queensland inquiry into that state's container scheme, and whether it would strengthen oversight of WA Return Recycle Renew Ltd. The Government said it was never formally notified of the findings and considers existing arrangements appropriate.
ask: When the WA Government received formal notification of the Queensland parliamentary inquiry findings into the Container Refund Scheme, whether the Department has assessed those findings and will table the assessment, which recommendations WA will implement, partially implement or not implement, whether the Government has considered Ministerial approval of WARRRL board appointments, an independent complaints mechanism and additional integrity and accountability measures for WARRRL and what it determined, and whether the Minister has any role in approving or reviewing appointments to the WARRRL board.
answer: The Government said the State Government was not formally notified by the Queensland Government of the findings of the Queensland Parliamentary Inquiry into the Queensland Container Refund Scheme, and that the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation undertook a review of the report. It said the Queensland recommendations relate to the Queensland Container Refund Scheme rather than the Western Australian scheme, that the two operate under different legislative and governance arrangements, and that the Queensland Parliamentary Inquiry noted a number of features of the Western Australian governance framework favourably. It said it considers the existing governance, integrity and accountability arrangements for WA Return Recycle Renew Ltd to be appropriate. It said the Minister for the Environment's role is to approve two members of the nine member board, being the Chair and the Community Representative, both of whom must be independent of the waste and beverage industry, and that the composition of the board is such that major beverage companies cannot form a majority.
finding: The Government did not identify a single Queensland recommendation it will adopt, and offered no independent complaints mechanism. The Minister approves two of the nine board members. Its statement that the Queensland inquiry viewed the Western Australian framework favourably is not sourced to any passage of that report.

title: THE SCHEME'S COST TO WINE, SPIRITS AND BEER
summary: Bevan asked whether the Government had assessed the cost of the scheme to wine producers, craft distillers and independent brewers, modelled the Wine Equalisation Tax effect, or would support a deferral. The Government answered no on the modelling and referred every other part elsewhere.
ask: Whether the Government has assessed the impact of Container Deposit Scheme costs on wine producers, craft distillers and independent brewers, whether it has modelled the impact of the Wine Equalisation Tax on the effective cost of the scheme for wine producers, whether it has considered any exemption, rebate, transitional assistance or alternative levy for small beverage producers and what options, whether it has assessed the competitive impact on WA producers of wine and spirits inclusion occurring ahead of reforms in South Australia, Victoria and New South Wales, and whether it will support a deferral of wine and spirits inclusion or, if not, what measures it will implement before 1 July 2026 to mitigate the impact on small producers.
answer: Asked whether it had undertaken any modelling of the impact of the Wine Equalisation Tax on the effective cost of the scheme for wine producers, the Government answered no. It answered the question on impact assessments by referring to Legislative Assembly Question on Notice 2634, the questions on exemptions, rebates and transitional assistance and on a deferral by referring to Question on Notice 2576, and the question on competitive impact by referring to Question on Notice 2584.
finding: No modelling of how the Wine Equalisation Tax compounds the scheme cost was done. The competitive impact question was referred to an answer about how many producers had signed an agreement, and the deferral question was referred to an answer that does not mention a deferral.

title: WHAT PRODUCERS WERE TOLD VS WHAT THEY SIGNED
summary: Bevan asked when the regulations were gazetted, how many producers had been issued with and had signed a Supply Agreement on three dates in May, and whether producers may have relied on information given at industry sessions that the signed agreement then superseded. The Government gave the gazettal date and answered no on reliance.
ask: When the regulations including wine and spirits containers in the scheme were gazetted, how many wine producers had been issued a supply agreement and how many had executed one as at 1, 7 and 28 May 2026, how many were expected to need one before 1 July 2026, whether WARRRL held industry information sessions on 7 and 28 May 2026 and will table the presentations, guidance and written responses from them, whether clauses 17.11 and 17.12 provide that prior representations are superseded by the executed agreement, and whether the Government has assessed whether producers who attended those sessions may have relied on information that would not form part of the legally binding agreement.
answer: The Government said the regulations were gazetted on 15 April 2026. It answered the questions on how many wine producers had been issued with or had executed a Supply Agreement by referring to Legislative Assembly Question on Notice 2629. It said the questions about industry information sessions relate to information controlled by WA Return Recycle Renew Ltd and that access should be sought from that company, which it described as a private company. It said the question on the effect of clauses 17.11 and 17.12 seeks a legal interpretation and cited Standing Order 77(2). Asked whether it had assessed whether producers attending information sessions before receiving a Supply Agreement may have relied on information that would not form part of the legally binding agreement, it answered no.
finding: The regulations were gazetted on 15 April 2026, 77 days before commencement. The Government has not assessed whether producers relied on information given at industry sessions that the signed agreement then superseded, and the material from those sessions was placed beyond reach as a private company's documents.

title: FPC REVENUE RESTING ON EXPIRING SANDALWOOD
summary: Bevan asked the Forest Products Commission to break down its forecast Sale of Goods and Services revenue, state its sandalwood harvest and revenue assumptions across the forward estimates, and quantify the impact if sandalwood harvesting ceased. The Government provided the figures.
ask: For a breakdown of the Forest Products Commission's Sale of Goods and Services revenue by plantation, ecological thinning and sandalwood operations for 2025-26 and 2026-27, the assumed sandalwood harvest tonnages and revenue across the forward estimates, what proportion of the 2026-27 forecast depends on sandalwood harvesting after the current Order expires in December 2026, the calculations behind the estimated 10 per cent profit reduction from changed sandalwood access, the forecast impact on revenue, profit, employees and contractors if sandalwood harvesting ceased, the principal sources of the forecast revenue increase despite reduced sandalwood activity, the assumed timber supply and revenue if the Wesbeam State Agreement expires, and the projected pine sawlog volumes available for sale.
answer: The Government said 2026-27 sales of goods and services revenue by operational area is plantation operations $105.385 million, native forest $7.340 million and sandalwood operations $16.304 million, a total of $129.029 million, against a 2025-26 estimated actual total of $111.463 million. It said assumed sandalwood harvest volumes are 1,400 tonnes in 2025-26, 474 tonnes in 2026-27, 1,400 tonnes in 2027-28, 1,400 tonnes in 2028-29 and 400 tonnes in 2029-30, with assumed revenue of $16.212 million in 2025-26, $16.304 million in 2026-27 and $18.000 million in each of 2027-28, 2028-29 and 2029-30. It said the Commission assumed a limited harvest operation between June 2026 and December 2026 and utilisation of remaining inventory to June 2027. It said sandalwood profit before tax and biological movements is $0.935 million against Commission profit before tax and biological movements of $8.748 million, being 10.7 per cent. It said sandalwood overheads as a share of Commission overheads are 19 per cent in 2025-26, 15 per cent in 2026-27 and 2027-28, and 17 per cent in 2028-29 and 2029-30. It said that if sandalwood harvesting ceased, revenue, profit and contract expenses would reduce to zero. It said the Commission supplies Wesbeam under a contract of sale that terminates in 2029, that total forecast timber supply volume in 2029-30 is approximately 1 million tonnes, and that projected sawlog products are 594,000 tonnes in 2026-27, 596,000 tonnes in 2027-28, 660,000 tonnes in 2028-29 and 509,000 tonnes in 2029-30.
finding: Sandalwood carries 10.7 per cent of the Commission's profit and up to 19 per cent of its overheads, and the assumed harvest falls from 1,400 tonnes to 474 tonnes in 2026-27. The Commission confirmed that if harvesting ceased, sandalwood revenue, profit and contract expenses would reduce to zero, and that its outyear forecasts remain provisional pending Government decisions on sandalwood operations beyond 31 December 2026.

title: WHEN DOES THE GLOUCESTER TREE REOPEN
summary: Bevan asked when the Gloucester Tree will reopen and what its continued closure is doing to Pemberton tourism operators; the Government said reopening is imminent, gave no firm date, and pointed to alternative attractions and waived park fees.
ask: The anticipated reopening date for the Gloucester Tree, what works or approvals remain outstanding, whether partial reopening is possible, and the impact of the closure on Pemberton tourism and local businesses.
answer: The Government said the reopening of the Gloucester Tree is imminent, that installing new infrastructure into a living tree is highly complex and partial public access was not possible, and that contractors are installing the lookout structure. It said visitors could climb the Bicentennial Tree or use the Aerial Adventures Pemberton high ropes course, and that the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions had waived park entry fees to Gloucester National Park until the tree reopens.
finding: The Government said reopening is imminent but gave no firm date, and pointed to alternatives, the Bicentennial Tree and the high ropes course, and waived Gloucester National Park entry fees, without assessing the cost of the closure to Pemberton operators.

title: WHERE THE PRESCRIBED BURNING MONEY GOES
summary: Bevan asked for a five-year breakdown of prescribed burning and fire management spending, including aviation and the top suppliers; the Government gave the breakdown, showing supplies and services rising to $12.6 million a year with aviation the largest cost, but could not fully isolate all aviation spending.
ask: A five-year breakdown of supplies and services spending on prescribed burning and fire management, the top ten suppliers, aviation costs, and hectares treated by distance from populated places.
answer: The Government provided a five-year breakdown of Supplies and Services expenditure within Service 9 Prescribed Burning and Fire Management, totalling about $10.7 million in 2020-21 rising to $12.6 million in 2024-25, and listed its top suppliers, most of them aviation-related, including Helicopter Logistics ($7.29 million over five years), Frontier Helicopters ($4.66 million) and aviation fuel from Air BP ($2.53 million). It said it could not provide an exhaustive aviation breakdown because some ledger categories also capture non-aviation expenditure.
finding: The answer confirmed prescribed-burning supplies and services ran from about $10.7 million to $12.6 million a year, with aviation the single largest cost through helicopter hire and fuel, and that the Government could not fully separate all aviation spending because the ledgers mix it with other costs.

title: SINGLE POWER LINES INTO GROWING TOWNS
summary: Bevan asked why towns including Margaret River, Manjimup and Walpole are served by single transmission lines and what redundancy is planned; the Government confirmed Margaret River is on a single 66kV line and Beenup a single 132kV line, and pointed to general planning and a Busselton upgrade.
ask: How many outages have hit the Margaret River to Busselton, Beenup to Manjimup and Denmark to Walpole lines over ten years, why some towns rely on a single line, and what network resilience upgrades are planned.
answer: The Government said Denmark to Walpole is fed via the distribution network, that the Busselton to Margaret River line had seven outages averaging 9 hours 39 minutes and the Manjimup to Beenup line five outages averaging 15 hours 22 minutes, and that Margaret River zone substation is fed by a single 66kV circuit and Beenup by a single 132kV circuit, while Busselton and Manjimup each have two 66kV circuits and one 132kV circuit. It said Western Power plans the network under risk-based principles, publishes a Transmission System Plan, and is expanding the Busselton zone substation and upgrading the Picton-Capel line.
finding: The answer confirmed Margaret River runs on a single 66kV line and Beenup on a single 132kV line, with seven and five outages on those corridors, and pointed to general planning and a Busselton upgrade rather than a committed fix for the single-line towns.

title: DOES BOYUP BROOK GET ITS FPC RATES
summary: Bevan asked the Treasurer whether the Forest Products Commission's rates-equivalent payments for land in the Shire of Boyup Brook reach the shire in full; the Government confirmed rates were paid from 2020-21 to 2024-25 but said it does not hold the data at individual local-government level.
ask: Whether the Forest Products Commission has paid rates-equivalent amounts for land in the Shire of Boyup Brook, whether that money has been passed to the shire in full, and whether any shortfall against standard rates exists.
answer: The Government said the Forest Products Commission paid rates to the Shire of Boyup Brook between 2020-21 and 2024-25, and that the Department of Treasury and Finance's Strategic Information Management System does not contain this information at the level of individual local government authority.
finding: The Government confirmed the Forest Products Commission paid rates to the shire from 2020-21 to 2024-25, but said it does not hold the data at individual local-government level to show whether the shire received them in full or whether any shortfall exists.

title: NINETEEN BIOFUEL QUESTIONS, ONE-LINE ANSWER
summary: Across three questions to two ministers, Bevan asked nineteen detailed questions on biofuels from forestry and farm residues; each was answered with a single sentence that a strategy is being developed.
ask: Whether the State has a biofuels strategy, what assessment had been done of fuels from forestry and agricultural residues, and what funding, grants or Commonwealth opportunities had been pursued.
answer: To all nineteen questions, repeated across two further questions to the Minister for Agriculture and Food, the Government said only that, as announced at the 2025 election, it is currently developing a biofuels strategy.
finding: Nineteen specific questions on a regional industry opportunity were met with a single sentence and no detail.

title: THREE LICENCES IN A $40M SANDALWOOD INDUSTRY
summary: Bevan asked what funds and structures support the transition to an Aboriginal-led sandalwood industry; the Government confirmed $280,000 over three years, a dissolved advisory group and only three licences.
ask: What funding supports the transition to an Aboriginal-led sandalwood industry, which advisory body guides wild harvest, and why only three harvesters are licensed despite a doubled quota.
answer: The Government said it invested $280,000 over three years through a capability program, that the WA Sandalwood Advisory Group was dissolved in 2024 having fulfilled its functions, and that three regulation-67 licences are currently in place. It reported about $665,000 spent on compliance and 21.86 tonnes of illegally harvested sandalwood seized between 2021 and 2025.
finding: A $40 million industry meant to transition to Aboriginal leadership rests on $280,000, a dissolved advisory group and three current licences.

title: WESTPORT NOISE THRESHOLDS STILL NOT SET
summary: Bevan asked what underwater noise modelling and limits exist for the Westport works in Cockburn Sound; the Government said modelling is still in progress and thresholds are yet to be set.
ask: Whether baseline underwater acoustic modelling was done before Westport works, whether defined noise limits for pile-driving and dredging exist, and what protects dolphins during breeding periods.
answer: The Government said independent baseline noise studies are published and that construction and operational modelling is in progress, with any acoustic threshold limits to be informed later by the Environmental Protection Authority and Commonwealth agencies.
finding: Noise limits to protect dolphins are described as something to be set later, not figures that exist now.

title: WESTPORT DOLPHIN ASSESSMENT 'IN PROGRESS'
summary: Bevan asked what baseline data exists on Cockburn Sound's dolphins and how the precautionary principle was applied; the Government said the assessment is still in progress.
ask: Whether the Sound is recognised as dolphin breeding habitat, what baseline population data exists, whether behavioural displacement from noise was assessed, and how the precautionary principle was applied.
answer: The Government said the State and Commonwealth environmental impact assessment processes for the future container port at Kwinana are in progress.
finding: Specific questions on dolphin habitat, baseline data and the precautionary principle were answered only by stating the assessment is ongoing.

title: WESTPORT OVERSIGHT AND REMEDIATION TO COME
summary: Bevan asked what independent oversight and remediation provisions exist for irreversible harm at Westport; the Government described panels and assessment processes still being settled.
ask: What independent scientific panels review Westport's environmental risk, whether all modelling will be public before approval, and what remediation exists if dolphin populations decline after construction.
answer: The Government pointed to the Western Australian Marine Studies Institute Westport Marine Science Program and specialist panels, public environmental review processes, enforceable approval conditions, and remediation provisions to be set through State and Commonwealth approvals.
finding: Oversight structures exist, but the accountability for irreversible harm and the remediation provisions are still to be determined through the approvals process.

title: PENGUIN ISLAND CENTRE CLOSED AND DEMOLISHED
summary: Bevan asked when the Penguin Island Discovery Centre was closed and demolished and how $3.3 million was spent; the Government gave the dates and confirmed the centre will not be rebuilt on the island.
ask: When the Discovery Centre was closed and demolished, how the roughly $3 million allocated for it was spent, and what the current little penguin population is.
answer: The Government said closure was announced in August 2022, the decision not to rebuild on the island and to demolish was announced on 26 August 2022 with works from February 2024, and that of $3.3 million originally allocated, funding was reallocated to demolition, habitat rehabilitation and a mainland feasibility study. It put the 2024 penguin population at 74 to 128 individuals.
finding: The island lost both its visitor centre and any rebuild, while the penguin population it was built around now sits in the low hundreds at most.

title: FERRY ACCESS DREDGED, NO IMPACT ASSESSED
summary: Bevan asked about sand build-up affecting ferry access to Penguin Island and the cost to the operator; the Government gave dredging costs but had not assessed the operator's losses.
ask: What works addressed sand build-up affecting ferry access, how many days of service disruption occurred, and whether the financial impact on the operator had been assessed.
answer: The Government said DBCA removed sand around the jetty in 2024 and 2025 at a cost of $142,821 and $37,505, that there are no formal navigation channels and so no access assessment, and that it does not record when the operator chooses not to run the ferry. It had not assessed the operator's financial impact.
finding: The Government funded dredging but did not assess what restricted access has cost the commercial operator who depends on it.

title: TIGHTER ACCESS RULES, IMPACT NOT MEASURED
summary: Bevan asked what visitor restrictions had been added at Penguin Island since 2016 and their cumulative impact on the tour operator; the Government listed the changes but had not measured the commercial effect.
ask: What seasonal closures and conservation restrictions had been added since 2016, what consultation occurred with the operator, and whether the cumulative commercial impact had been assessed.
answer: The Government listed changes including a four-week extension to the annual breeding-season closure, hot-weather closures above 35 degrees, speed restrictions and habitat works, and said it consults closely with the operator. It said the operator makes its own commercial decisions, without providing an impact assessment.
finding: Access has been progressively tightened since 2016, but the cumulative effect on the licensed tourism operator has not been measured.

title: NO PLAN IF THE TOUR OPERATOR GOES UNDER
summary: Bevan asked whether the Government had assessed the regional economic impact if Perth Wildlife Encounters ceased; the Government said it does not assess individual operators.
ask: Whether the regional economic impact of the operator ceasing had been assessed, the employment it supports, and whether any contingency planning had been done for operator insolvency.
answer: The Government said Tourism WA does not assess the economic contribution of individual operators, but noted it engages through DBCA stakeholder meetings and has assisted the operator's efforts toward sustainability.
finding: The Government has no assessment of what the region loses if the operator fails, and no contingency plan for that outcome.

title: NORTHCLIFFE WATER CARTED IN AT $569 A DAY
summary: Bevan asked what it costs to keep carting water into Northcliffe; the Government confirmed the town still has no permanent supply, with trucked-in water running at $569 a day.
ask: How many kilolitres of water are carted to Northcliffe each day, what it costs, and the total spent over the years the town has gone without a permanent supply.
answer: The Government said about 41 kilolitres a day in November 2025 at $569 per day, with a cumulative cost of $3,095,740 since 2010-11, and noted the arrangement began under the previous Liberal-National Government.
finding: Northcliffe has relied on trucked-in water for more than a decade at over $3 million, and the answer confirmed the cost but offered no permanent supply.

title: PERTH WATCH HOUSE OVER CAPACITY ON 95 DAYS
summary: Bevan asked about custodial staffing and watch house overcrowding; the Government confirmed the Perth Watch House exceeded its design capacity on 95 days, peaking at 131 detainees on Boxing Day.
ask: How custodial and watch house staffing had changed since January 2025, how Protective Service Officers are being used in lock-ups, and how often the Perth Watch House had exceeded its capacity.
answer: The Government said staffing had "increased" without giving a figure, that Protective Service Officers are deployed as operationally required, and that between January 2025 and January 2026 the Perth Watch House exceeded its design capacity of 72 on 95 days, reaching a peak of 131 detainees on Boxing Day.
finding: A facility built for 72 held up to 131 people and was over capacity on 95 days, while the staffing question was answered only with the word "increased."

title: $8.9M ON REGIONAL COURT SECURITY, NO ANALYSIS
summary: Bevan asked what regional court security contractors cost and whether a cost-benefit analysis against auxiliary police had been done; the Government gave the figure and confirmed no analysis exists.
ask: The cost of contracted regional court security in the past year, whether any cost-benefit analysis against using auxiliary police had been done, and what regional justice programs had been reduced.
answer: The Government said contracted court security cost $8,942,063 from November 2024 to October 2025, confirmed no cost-benefit analysis had been undertaken, and noted an Aboriginal-led family violence court in Broome had been delayed by the existing court building.
finding: Nearly $9 million a year is spent on contractors with no analysis of whether auxiliary police would be cheaper, while a regional family violence court is delayed.

title: $29M DROUGHT HIT TO THE PLANTATION ESTATE
summary: Bevan asked why softwood plantations were so vulnerable to drought and why thinning performance is no longer reported; the Government confirmed a $29 million valuation hit and that it will not reinstate the thinning measure.
ask: Why the State's softwood plantations were so vulnerable to drought, how much of the asset value was lost, and why the thinning timeliness measure was dropped from the annual report.
answer: The Government said about 1,500 hectares in the South-West and 6,000 in the Mid-West were significantly affected, with a roughly $29 million negative impact on plantation value, that the thinning indicators were updated under the Government Trading Enterprises Act, and that it would not reinstate the thinning timeliness measure.
finding: The Government confirmed a $29 million drought hit to the estate and declined to restore the public measure that tracks whether plantations are thinned on time.

title: ERADICATION OF SHOT-HOLE BORER ABANDONED
summary: Bevan asked for the advice behind giving up on eradicating the polyphagous shot-hole borer and what it has cost; the Government confirmed eradication was deemed not feasible after almost $60 million spent.
ask: Whether the expert advice to abandon eradication of the polyphagous shot-hole borer would be tabled, how much had been spent each year, and whether the infestation can be contained.
answer: The Government said the National Management Group decided eradication was no longer technically feasible, reported national cost-sharing expenditure rising to about $25 million in 2024-25, and confirmed 1,628 sites identified with 1,522 treated. It said the pest cannot be contained long-term.
finding: After almost $60 million across the response, eradication has been abandoned and the program now aims only to slow a pest that cannot be contained.

title: NO AUDITS ON BUILDERS' SUPPORT LOANS
summary: Bevan asked whether builders who received state support loans had been audited and how long building disputes take; the Government said no audits had been done and key data is not collected.
ask: Whether builders that received loans under the Builders' Support Facility had been audited, how long building disputes take to resolve, and how many homes have been under construction for more than four years.
answer: The Government said no compliance audits had been undertaken, that building disputes averaged 177 days to resolve in 2024-25 with a review of contract laws due in late 2026, and that data on builds running longer than four years "is not collected."
finding: Public loans to builders have gone unaudited, and the Government does not collect the data needed to see how many families are stuck in years-long builds.

title: DENMARK STUDENTS LEARN ARTS IN OLD HOUSING
summary: Bevan asked whether Denmark Senior High School's music and drama rooms, set up in repurposed houses, meet arts-learning standards; the Government confirmed no full assessment was done.
ask: Whether the repurposed residential buildings used as the school's music and drama classrooms had been assessed against the minimum design standards for arts learning, and whether the school was in any capital works plan.
answer: The Government said the rooms were inspected in 2022 but "a full detailed assessment for new facilities was not undertaken," listed mould remediation works including sub-floor ventilation, drainage and dehumidifiers, and declined the capital works question under Standing Order 77 and Cabinet confidentiality.
finding: The rooms were never assessed against the standard for the subjects taught in them, and the Government is patching moisture problems rather than replacing the buildings.

title: SMALL MILLS COMPETE WHILE BIG FIRMS NEGOTIATE
summary: Bevan asked for the first native-forest timber production data under the new plan and how logs are allocated; the Government detailed contracts and confirmed large firms can negotiate private treaty.
ask: How much native forest timber has been committed under the new Forest Management Plan, whether large firms negotiate private-treaty contracts while small businesses compete, and whether the best commercial price is being achieved.
answer: The Government reported 49 contracts and committed volumes by grade, said all businesses had been offered private-treaty contracts or restricted tenders, and confirmed Simcoa took 79 per cent of mine-site clearing wood. It said no independent value-for-money analysis was done.
finding: The Government confirmed it sells timber by private treaty without independent analysis that the public is getting best value.

title: TIMBER LOSES ITS ENVIRONMENTAL CERTIFICATION
summary: Bevan asked which forest products remain environmentally certified; the Government confirmed mine-site, eucalypt-plantation and hardwood-plantation timber are not certified.
ask: Which forest products sold by the Forest Products Commission remain independently certified, which are not, and whether the Commission would recommence certification to give suppliers and the public assurance.
answer: The Government said softwood, sandalwood and ecological thinning products are certified to AS 4708, but timber from mine-site clearing and eucalypt sharefarm plantations is not, and that hardwood plantation timber is uncertified because there has not been sufficient market demand to justify the cost.
finding: Timber that was once certified as sustainably managed now reaches buyers, including those who require certification, without it.

title: SAWLOGS FROM MINE SITES FALL SHORT OF MILLS
summary: Bevan asked how high-value logs from mine-site clearing are recovered and supplied to sawmills; the Government confirmed supply sits below what mills request.
ask: What volume of high-value logs is recovered from mine-site clearing, whether all are supplied to sawmills for value adding, and whether current supply keeps the sawmill sector viable.
answer: The Government reported 235,000 tonnes of forest products sold from mine-site clearing, including about 6,000 tonnes of high-value recovery logs, said recovery is done by the mine operator with the Commission marketing the logs, and confirmed contracted supply is below the upper limit mills request.
finding: The high-value log supply that mills depend on is recovered by mining companies and falls short of what sawmills ask for.

title: WHO WAS CONSULTED ON THE ART AND SURROGACY BILL
summary: Bevan asked which women's advocacy groups were consulted on the ART and Surrogacy Bill and whether independent women's-rights advocates sat on the expert panel; the answer described general consultation without naming them.
ask: Which women's advocacy groups or independent women's-rights experts were invited to consult on the Assisted Reproductive Technology and Surrogacy Bill, and why independent women's-rights advocates were not included on the Ministerial Expert Panel.
answer: The Government said the Bill rests on the 2018 Sonia Allan Review and a 2022 expert panel review, both open to all bodies including women's interest groups, and that panel members completed conflict-of-interest forms. It did not name specific women's-rights groups or address why independent women's-rights advocates were not on the panel.
finding: Asked who specifically was consulted, the Government pointed to broad review processes and left the named-group and panel-composition questions unanswered.

title: SIX PER CENT OF THE PLANTATION TARGET MET
summary: Bevan put it to the Government that after three years the $350 million plantation program had reached only 6 per cent of the 35,000 hectares promised; the answer did not confirm the original target would be met.
ask: Whether the Government will achieve the 35,000 hectare plantation target originally promised, why the Forest Products Commission has been so slow, and whether progress will be reviewed publicly.
answer: The Government reframed the program as a record $350 million over ten years, said about 20,000 to 25,000 hectares is likely if focused on freehold land, and noted 1,538 hectares established through joint ventures. It did not commit to the original 35,000 hectare figure.
finding: Confronted with 6 per cent delivery against the promised area, the Government lowered the expectation rather than confirming the original target.

title: ELECTION PROMISES MISSING FROM THE BUDGET PAPERS
summary: Bevan asked where six named election promises sit in the budget papers; several were not located and one was confirmed as not funded.
ask: Where the Denmark Primary School car park, the Manjimup Rea Park redevelopment, the Margaret River fire station, regional childcare support and the Boyup Brook Recreation Centre are funded in the budget, given none appears as a specific line item.
answer: The Government confirmed $5.1 million spent on the Margaret River fire station and $5.1 million for regional childcare, said the Boyup Brook Recreation Centre is not funded, and left several of the other named promises without a budget location.
finding: Asked to point to the line items for promised projects, the Government could account for some, confirmed one was not funded, and did not locate the rest.

title: NO BUDGET LINE FOR THE THREE HOSPITAL ASKS
summary: Bevan asked where the budget funds Margaret River Hospital works, a Manjimup CT scanner and the Bridgetown reroof; the answer listed other projects and named none of the three.
ask: Whether the budget includes works for Margaret River Hospital, funding for a Manjimup CT scanner, and the $1 million Bridgetown Hospital emergency department reroof, and the assumptions behind year-on-year cuts to ambulance and patient transport.
answer: The Government listed regional health investments including $471 million for the Bunbury Hospital redevelopment and a virtual emergency department expansion, said urgent care clinics are a federal initiative, and stated ambulance funding would be maintained over the forward estimates. It did not identify funding for any of the three Warren-Blackwood items asked about.
finding: Three specific local hospital asks were answered with a list of other projects, none of which were the ones in the question.

title: MARGARET RIVER HIGH STAGE 2 LEFT TO CABINET
summary: Bevan asked whether the budget funds Margaret River Senior High stage 2 and three other schools; the stage 2 answer cited Cabinet confidentiality.
ask: Whether the budget funds stage 2 of the Margaret River Senior High School expansion, the $12 million Cowaramup classroom block, and maintenance at Bridgetown and Boyup Brook schools.
answer: On stage 2, the Government said it is inappropriate to comment on Cabinet deliberations. On Cowaramup it said funding progresses staged delivery with further funding sought in future budgets. It confirmed a $20,000 sports shed for Bridgetown and no funding for Boyup Brook District High School.
finding: The flagship ask, stage 2 of an overcrowded high school, was deflected to Cabinet confidentiality, and Boyup Brook received nothing.

title: 'UNCLEAR WHAT FUNDING' FOR OVERTAKING LANES
summary: Bevan asked whether the budget funds overtaking lanes between Manjimup and Bridgetown; the Minister said it was unclear what funding he meant.
ask: Whether the budget funds the implementation of overtaking lanes between Manjimup and Bridgetown, where it sits and what it includes.
answer: The Government replied that "it is unclear what funding the Member is referring to."
finding: A direct question about overtaking lanes was returned as a question, with no figure and no location in the budget.

title: 7.32 RANGER FTE FOR LEEUWIN-NATURALISTE
summary: Bevan asked how many Aboriginal Ranger Program FTEs work in Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park; the Government gave the funded figure but noted FTEs are not allocated per park.
ask: Whether the Aboriginal Ranger Program funds rangers working within Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park, and if so how many FTEs and on what timeline.
answer: The Government said the program is tenure-blind and funds organisations per FTE rather than per park. It funds the Undalup Association for 7.32 FTE to work across several areas including Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park.
finding: The park is covered by a single funded organisation whose 7.32 FTE are shared across multiple sites, not dedicated to it.

title: AGED CARE ASSESSMENT FUNDING DROPS TO ZERO
summary: Bevan asked why the aged care assessment line fell to zero and why palliative care funding was discontinued; the Government described short-term Commonwealth contracts ending in 2026.
ask: Why the Aged Care Assessment allocation dropped from $10.2 million to zero across the forward estimates, and why Comprehensive Palliative Care in Aged Care funding was discontinued.
answer: The Government said a 12-month state and Commonwealth contract continues aged care assessments, to be reflected in the mid-year review, and that two palliative care projects continue under a Commonwealth partnership only until 30 June 2026, with no commitment beyond that date.
finding: Both services rest on short-term contracts running to 2026, with no funding shown beyond, in budget lines that read as zero.

title: FIVE STAYING-IN-PLACE HUBS IN WARREN-BLACKWOOD
summary: Bevan asked whether Warren-Blackwood is included in the Staying in Place program; the Government confirmed five existing hubs and two more approved.
ask: Which areas benefit from the Assisting Staying in Place to Thrive program, whether Warren-Blackwood is included, and what data underpins the limited budget allocation.
answer: The Government said there are five existing Staying in Place hubs in the electorate assisted by the initiative, with two further hubs approved for start-up support, and that $250,000 in state funding was approved following a request from Linkwest to expand the program.
finding: The program reaches the electorate through seven hubs, funded by a one-off $250,000 expansion rather than ongoing support.

title: THINNING COSTS EXPECTED TO EXCEED REVENUE
summary: Bevan asked for a forensic breakdown of the forestry budget; the Government confirmed costs of the ecological thinning program are expected to exceed revenue.
ask: For the 2025-26 revenue breakdown by operation, the cumulative shortfall on ecological thinning, and how much land the $350 million softwood fund will ultimately buy.
answer: The Government gave 2025-26 timber revenue as plantations $88.1 million (79 per cent), native forest $7.2 million (6 per cent) and sandalwood $16.2 million (15 per cent), said costs of ecological thinning are anticipated to exceed revenues by more than $5 million, and estimated the softwood fund would secure about 20,000 to 25,000 hectares of freehold land.
finding: The Government confirmed the thinning program runs at a loss and that the $350 million plantation fund will fall well short of the area once promised.

title: WHO PROFITS FROM THE GNANGARA CARBON CREDITS
summary: Bevan asked why the State is buying land for carbon offsets while a private entity replants Gnangara for its own carbon benefit, and what the reservation costs the State; most of it was redirected to the Forestry Minister.
ask: Why the State is purchasing land for carbon offsetting while a private entity replants Gnangara for its own carbon credits, whether the Forest Products Commission is compensating Wesbeam for the reservation, and the total cost to the State.
answer: The Government said no commercial terms had been agreed on the Carbon for Conservation proposal and that DBCA is considering carbon farming on the conservation estate. The questions on compensation and total cost were referred to the Minister for Forestry.
finding: The core questions on who profits from the carbon credits and what the reservation costs the public were passed to another minister rather than answered.

title: 13,000 HECTARES OF GNANGARA STILL UNREHABILITATED
summary: Bevan asked what rehabilitation had been done at Gnangara since pine removal began; the Government confirmed about 13,000 hectares remain unrehabilitated.
ask: What rehabilitation DBCA had undertaken at Gnangara since pine removal began in 2004, how many hectares remain unrehabilitated, and why the pines were reserved rather than re-established for production.
answer: The Government said about 5,000 hectares of native vegetation had been planted since 2004 while roughly 13,000 hectares across Yanchep, Gnangara and Pinjar remain unrehabilitated, with the remaining pines now managed to maximise cone production as a food source for Carnaby's cockatoo.
finding: More than two decades after pine removal began, about 13,000 hectares remain unrehabilitated, with management now driven by cockatoo food rather than timber.

title: 165,000 CUBIC METRES OF TIMBER LOCKED UP
summary: Bevan asked what timber volume was lost when Gnangara was reserved and how Wesbeam's supply is being maintained; the Government detailed the standing volume and a private-treaty karri arrangement.
ask: What volume of timber was lost to the Gnangara reservation and its value, whether the Forest Products Commission can meet its supply contracts to Wesbeam, and on what basis Wesbeam receives karri logs.
answer: The Government said about 165,000 cubic metres of LVL log and 24,000 cubic metres of industrial wood were standing at the time of the cessation, with "no market value as it is not available to harvest." It said karri supply to Wesbeam was tendered to 2023 and has since been by private treaty at the equivalent pine price, with tonnages declining year on year.
finding: A large standing timber resource was reserved, and the shortfall is being covered in part by karri sold to Wesbeam on a private-treaty basis rather than competitive tender.

title: ECOLOGICAL THINNING LOGS SOLD BY PRIVATE TREATY
summary: Bevan asked how ecological thinning is costed and how its logs are sold; the Government confirmed most contracts were privately negotiated and named the companies.
ask: Whether the ecological thinning prescription was published, what the program costs per hectare, whether contracts were tendered, and how stockpiled logs are sold.
answer: The Government put jarrah thinning at about $10,500 per hectare and karri at about $13,500, said contractors were not selected by public tender, and confirmed that aside from tendered firewood and sawlog, all other thinning timber sales were privately negotiated. It listed the businesses awarded private-treaty contracts and reported about 62,000 tonnes held in timber reserves.
finding: A publicly funded thinning program is selling most of its timber through privately negotiated contracts rather than open tender.

title: $350M PLANTATION PLAN, NO REGIONAL ALLOCATION
summary: Bevan asked how much of the $350 million softwood plantation expansion has reached Warren-Blackwood; the Government said it does not allocate by region.
ask: How much of the $350 million committed to expanding softwood plantations has been allocated to Warren-Blackwood, what consultation occurred with local government, and how many hectares have been planted.
answer: The Government said there are no specific allocations by region, with sites chosen on rainfall, soil, distance to market and price. It listed plantation established in the region from January 2022 to May 2025: Boyup Brook 1,505 hectares, Manjimup 402, Nannup 151, Bridgetown-Greenbushes 55 and Donnybrook-Balingup 0.
finding: After three years of a $350 million program, the region had about 2,113 hectares planted, and the Government does not track the spend by region at all.

title: NO DATA ON VOLUNTEER-ONLY AMBULANCE CALLOUTS
